476: Location exerted a highly significant effect on manganese. The highest value, 0.133 mg/kg, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 0.132 mg/kg and Nadia with 0.093 mg/kg. Birbhum/Howrah and Purba Bardhaman shared a common letter group, the difference between them being too small to be regarded as real, while the gap between the superior and inferior locations amounted to 0.040 mg/kg.
478: The three landraces likewise differed, the varietal effect being highly significant. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value, 0.120 mg/kg, followed by Gobindabhog with 0.120 mg/kg and Kalojira with 0.117 mg/kg. Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog shared a common letter and were thus on par with each other, while Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 0.003 mg/kg.
480: The effect of storage on manganese was non-significant. In order of sampling, the values were 0.119 mg/kg in fresh paddy, 0.119 mg/kg at 4 months, 0.119 mg/kg at 8 months and 0.120 mg/kg at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 12 months and the minimum at 4 months. Over the full year the value increased by 0.5%.
482: The interaction between location and variety was highly significant. Gobindabhog at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 0.143 mg/kg, and Radhunipagal at Nadia the inferior one with 0.088 mg/kg. The ranking of the landraces was not conserved across locations: at Nadia the order was Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; at Purba Bardhaman, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Kalojira, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog. Rank reversal of this kind establishes that the landraces did not respond uniformly to the three growing environments.
483: The interaction between location and storage was non-significant. The highest mean, 0.133 mg/kg, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 12 months and the lowest, 0.092 mg/kg, for Nadia at 8 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +0.4% at Nadia, +0.8% at Purba Bardhaman and +0.3% at Birbhum/Howrah. The three locations changed by closely comparable margins, storage having acted upon the grain in much the same manner irrespective of where it was grown.
484: The interaction between variety and storage was non-significant. The highest mean, 0.121 mg/kg, was recorded for Radhunipagal in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.117 mg/kg, for Kalojira at 8 months. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +0.7% in Gobindabhog, -0.4% in Radhunipagal and +1.2% in Kalojira. All three landraces shifted by nearly equivalent margins, storage having affected them alike.
485: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 0.146 mg/kg was recorded by Gobindabhog grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 0.087 mg/kg by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 8 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these two extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
492: Manganese behaved as the other minerals did, being unaffected by storage and determined entirely during the growing season. The varietal range was narrow, which most probably indicates that genetic control over manganese uptake is weaker in these landraces than for iron or zinc, where the differences extended to several fold. Soil therefore counted for considerably more than seed in respect of this element. The differences between sites are most probably governed by soil reaction and redox status, since manganese availability rises sharply as a flooded soil becomes reduced and anoxic; differences in the duration for which the fields were kept submerged constitute the most likely explanation. The interaction between site and landrace, while significant, involved very small absolute differences and carries little practical importance, although it does confirm that soil conditions rather than landrace determine the manganese content of the grain (Li et al., 2018).
495: The amino acid profile was determined on freshly harvested grain alone; the samples drawn at 4, 8 and 12 months were not assayed for these parameters. The results presented below therefore characterise the influence of location and variety on the amino acids of fresh grain. No inference is drawn regarding the effect of storage, that effect not having been measured. All fifteen amino acids are presented together in Table 24, and the SEm and CD figures given there pertain to the varietal means.
498: The effect of location was non-significant for fourteen of the fifteen amino acids, proline constituting the sole exception. For every other amino acid the three locations differed by less than 0.0025 mg/100 mg, a margin far too small to be of consequence. Proline attained 0.3000 mg/100 mg at Purba Bardhaman, 0.2967 mg/100 mg at Nadia and 0.2954 mg/100 mg at Birbhum/Howrah. Phenylalanine exhibited the widest spread among the non-significant traits at 0.0023 mg/100 mg.
500: The varietal effect was highly significant for every one of the fifteen amino acids. Gobindabhog carried the greatest quantity of thirteen amino acids, followed by Radhunipagal and, in third position, Kalojira. Glutamic acid was the most abundant amino acid in all three landraces, at 1.4690 mg/100 mg in Gobindabhog, 1.1983 mg/100 mg in Radhunipagal and 1.1141 mg/100 mg in Kalojira. Threonine was the least abundant, at 0.2770, 0.1898 and 0.1368 mg/100 mg respectively.
501: Two exceptions to the general order were recorded. Kalojira carried much the greatest quantity of cysteine, 1.6729 mg/100 mg against 0.9240 mg/100 mg in Gobindabhog, and ranked second for tyrosine. Cysteine and tyrosine were barely detectable in Radhunipagal, at 0.0017 and 0.0014 mg/100 mg respectively, values lying at the lower limit of the method's determination.
502: The magnitude of the varietal margin differed considerably between amino acids. Glutamic acid varied least, Gobindabhog exceeding Kalojira by 32%, while alanine varied most among the ordinary amino acids, at 141%. Summed over all fifteen amino acids, Gobindabhog carried 7.6407 mg/100 mg, Kalojira 5.4210 mg/100 mg and Radhunipagal 4.0672 mg/100 mg.
504: The interaction between location and variety was non-significant for thirteen of the fifteen amino acids, tyrosine and isoleucine constituting the two exceptions; for both, the ranking of the landraces was conserved at all three locations. The interaction therefore reflects a change in the width of the margins and not in their direction. Storage was not assayed for these parameters, so no interaction involving storage period is reported.
509: Three features of these results require explanation. The first is that growing site altered only proline while landrace altered every amino acid. The most probable reason is that amino acid composition is determined by the proportions in which the grain deposits its storage protein fractions, and those proportions are under genetic control, whereas soil and weather govern the quantity of protein accumulated rather than its composition. The present data are consistent with this interpretation, since growing site was material for soluble protein but not for the amino acids incorporated within it, and Devi et al. (2024) reached the same conclusion for maize. Because glutelin dominates the protein of milled rice (Jayaprakash et al., 2022), the amino acids of that fraction vary least between landraces while those belonging to the smaller prolamin fraction vary most, which is precisely the pattern obtained here. The second feature is the unusually high cysteine content of the pigmented landrace. Cysteine is concentrated in the globulin fraction (Jayaprakash et al., 2022), a bran and embryo protein, and the same landrace also led for ash and for fat in this study; all three observations indicate a proportionately thicker bran, and therefore a larger globulin share, as the most probable cause. The near-absence of cysteine and tyrosine in one landrace is more likely a failure of detection than a genuine absence and should be verified against the raw chromatograms. The third feature is that proline ran counter to aroma. Free proline in the developing grain is consumed in the synthesis of 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline (Luo et al., 2020; Renuka et al., 2022; Imran et al., 2023), so that the most fragrant landrace probably diverts proline into the aroma pathway rather than incorporating it into storage protein, which would leave it lowest in the bound form determined here. The remaining results conformed to expectation. All the essential amino acids were present, which supports the long-established view that rice protein is of good quality despite its low lysine content (Mahadevamma and Tharanathan, 2007); threonine ranked among the least abundant, as in other cereals (Devi et al., 2024); the branched-chain amino acids followed the order reported by Sui et al. (2023); and much of the aspartic acid, glutamic acid and glycine resides in the germ and outer layers (Kamjijam et al., 2020), so that the degree of milling will likewise condition the final profile.
513: The analysis of variance presented in the preceding sections treats each parameter in isolation and can indicate neither how the traits covary nor which treatments are alike in overall profile. Three further analyses were therefore undertaken: correlation analysis, principal component analysis and hierarchical cluster analysis. The same combination has been applied to rice quality data by Abdelsalam et al. (2025), who found the three methods to be mutually corroborative.
514: All three were based on the thirty six location by variety by storage treatment means, pooled over the two years, for the twenty three parameters in which storage was assayed. The fifteen amino acids were excluded, having been determined in fresh grain alone. It should be borne in mind that these analyses employ treatment means rather than individual replicate values, so that the coefficients describe the covariation of treatment means.
516: Correlation measures whether two traits rise and fall in concert: a positive value indicates movement in the same direction, a negative value that one rises as the other declines, and a value approaching zero that they vary independently. Coefficients were computed for all 253 pairs. With 36 pairs of values, a coefficient of 0.329 or greater is significant at the 5% level, and eighty seven pairs exceeded that threshold. The full matrix is presented in Figure 1.
517: Total phenol and total flavonoid were almost perfectly associated, for a straightforward reason: flavonoids constitute one family within the phenolic group, so that the two assays enumerate much of the same material twice. A laboratory constrained for time could determine either alone with negligible loss of information.
518: Total phenol, total flavonoid and antioxidant capacity constituted a tightly cohering block, as is to be expected, since phenolic compounds perform the greater part of the radical scavenging in rice grain. Shao et al. (2014) and Zhang et al. (2010) demonstrated these compounds to be concentrated in the bran and embryo of pigmented rice. Any landrace rich in one will therefore be rich in all three.
519: Aroma correlated strongly with fat, which ranks among the more instructive findings of the correlation analysis. Both declined during storage, and did so in concert, treatment by treatment. The probable explanation is that the two losses share a common cause: rice lipid is hydrolysed and oxidised in store, and the low-molecular-weight carbonyl compounds thereby generated impart the stale odour of old grain and act antagonistically to whatever fragrance remains. Zhou et al. (2002) described the same coupling between lipid breakdown and flavour change. Aroma was likewise associated with antioxidant capacity and with phenol, so that the entire complex of desirable traits rises and falls as a unit.
520: The strongest negative association obtained between amylose and soluble protein. The probable basis is competition for space: starch and protein are deposited within the same endosperm, so that a grain rich in one retains less of the other. Chattopadhyay et al. (2018) reported the same negative association in rice. Amylose was also negatively associated with antioxidant capacity and with fat; this reflects a storage effect rather than a compositional one, since amylose rose during storage while those two declined.
521: Among the minerals, copper and zinc were positively associated while copper and manganese were negatively associated. The probable explanation is that copper and zinc share part of their uptake route within the plant, whereas manganese behaves differently, its availability depending strongly upon the degree of flooding and reduction of the soil.
522: Two associations bear upon milling. Milling percentage and hulling were both correlated with total starch, since a grain well filled with starch is denser and withstands polishing more effectively. Head rice recovery correlated with ash and negatively with phytic acid, which points to grain anatomy, both of these reflecting the proportion of bran and aleurone within the kernel.
523: One practical implication emerges from the matrix as a whole. Aroma, fat, phenol, flavonoid, antioxidant capacity and soluble protein constitute a single tightly associated complex that declines in concert during storage, against which amylose moves inversely. A single judiciously chosen determination from within that complex would therefore afford a fair indication of the remainder, and in a screening programme would economise considerable laboratory effort.
